preamble: Seven solutions have something in common, not defined in their clues. All the other clues contain a letter superfluous to their solutions. In clue order, these letters form words that indicate the common theme.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; each light's entry one fifteensquared prints for it, the only choice of them whose crossings all agree; an entry not its answer carries the answer as its alteration's `from`

clue.text: Preaches, emitting a wild language

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so what is left is thrown into disorder
emitting means giving off, so the letter named after it is sent out of the word before

parts.note: taken as written; its R is this clue's superfluous letter, leaving peaches
taken as written, and given off

explanation.surface: A preacher gets carried away and starts shouting in tongues.
explanation.walkthrough: Without its superfluous R the clue reads 'Peaches, emitting a': PEACHES less A, rearranged, gives SPEECH. The R is the first letter of the hidden message.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech is spoken communication in words, so it serves as a synonym for language in general.

clue.text: Unproductive moan given title, it's said

indicators.note: it's said tells us to go by what is spoken rather than what is written

parts.note: with the O of moan superfluous this is a man given a title, a baron

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a pointless honour, as if a title were an empty reward.
explanation.walkthrough: The O of 'moan' is this clue's superfluous letter, leaving 'man given title'. Baron and barren are pronounced alike in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: Barren land or a barren woman yields no crops or offspring, so it means fruitless and unproductive.

clue.text: Grog, a load kept for festivity

parts.note: the run of letters across the words; its O, from load, is this clue's superfluous letter

explanation.surface: Barrels of rum laid in for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept' signals a run of letters held inside 'Grog, a load'; remove the superfluous O and it reads 'Grog, a lad', with GALA inside. Grog is rum and water, a sailor's drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive occasion or celebration, such as a special performance or a swimming gala.

clue.text: Archbishop almost by right

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the word for an archbishop is cut

parts.note: Thomas Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury murdered in his cathedral in 1170
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A churchman who is nearly always in the right.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven theme answers, so there is no definition and no superfluous letter: Boris Becker, the German tennis champion.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble's common theme is the first name Boris, and Boris Becker won Wimbledon at seventeen.

clue.text: Criminal clothing sunk by man facing questions

parts.note: with its K superfluous the word is sun, abbreviated S
Kim is a man's name, as in Kipling's novel
to ask is to question

explanation.surface: Clothes of a convicted man, sunk in the water while he faces interrogation.
explanation.walkthrough: The K of 'sunk' is this clue's superfluous letter. A man's name is a common way to clue a short set of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Robbers wear woollen face coverings with eye holes, made for skiing, to hide their identity in a raid.

clue.text: Eg a nice peer mobilised campaigning group

indicators.note: mobilised means set in motion, so the letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; its I is this clue's superfluous letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pleasant lord is roused into joining a protest movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder has eleven letters for a ten-letter answer; the extra I of 'nice' is the superfluous letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenpeace is the international environmental organisation known for direct-action protests at sea and elsewhere.

clue.text: Stakes sure to alter attitudes

parts.note: with its final S superfluous the word is stake, a post driven into the ground

indicators.note: to alter something is to change it, so these letters are changed in order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Gamblers' bets on a certainty can make people change their opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stakes' looks like bets, but read without its superfluous S it is a wooden post.
explanation.definitionFit: Postures are bodily positions or poses, and also adopted stances or opinions, just as attitudes can be either.

clue.text: Feature of cold maybe in a convenient amenity, lately being attraction

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in places the fish's feature inside the word for convenient

parts.note: fit as in suitable or convenient
with the L of cold superfluous this is a feature of cod, a fish

indicators.note: lately means at the end, so only the last letter of the word before is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A runny nose is the price of an open-air convenience, and somehow that is the attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: The L of 'cold' is this clue's superfluous letter: a cod is the fish, and its fin is the feature. 'Maybe' marks cod as one example of a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Affinity is a natural liking or sympathy for someone or something, a mutual pull or chemical attraction.

clue.text: Bet a clap disturbed calm

indicators.note: disturbed means upset or thrown out of place, so the letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written; its B is this clue's superfluous letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Eight letters of fodder for seven: the B of 'Bet' is the superfluous letter, and it starts the across part of the message.
explanation.definitionFit: To placate someone is to soothe or pacify them, so calm here is the verb meaning settle down.

clue.text: Prank swapping tips on holiday

parts.note: a lark is a prank or bit of fun

explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer, so no definition and no superfluous letter: Boris Karloff, the horror-film actor who played Frankenstein's monster.
explanation.definitionFit: The theme is the first name Boris, and Boris Karloff was the stage name of the English actor William Pratt.

clue.text: A void anger in European with old currency set aside

parts.note: this clue's superfluous letter: without it the clue begins 'void anger', or 'avoid anger' read as one word

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
the mark was the German currency before the euro

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'A void' as 'avoid' and the surface is about keeping calm; the A is the superfluous letter. The emptied anger joins on after E rather than sitting inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds is to reserve them for a particular purpose, so it means to put aside or allocate.

clue.text: Smear? It's affected experts with notes

parts.note: taken as written; its S is this clue's superfluous letter
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smear? It's' has eight letters for a seven-letter answer; the opening S is superfluous.
explanation.definitionFit: Maestri, the Italian plural of maestro, are distinguished conductors or musicians, masters of musical notes.

clue.text: Host with skill boards sides of curious light vehicles

indicators.note: to board is to get on or into, so the word for skill goes inside

parts.note: with its S superfluous the word is hot, and H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
art is skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A skilled host climbs aboard some odd-looking little carriages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' reads as a person, but the S is this clue's superfluous letter, leaving hot.
explanation.definitionFit: Handcarts are small carts pushed or pulled by hand, so they are light wheeled vehicles.

clue.text: An article's awfully close to repellent for one opposing devolution?

explanation.walkthrough: Eleven letters of fodder for ten: one A is superfluous, here taken from 'An'.
explanation.definitionFit: A centralist favours concentrating power in national government, so they resist handing powers to regions.

clue.text: Standard soon obtained with current dialect

explanation.definitionFit: Parsi, also spelt Parsee, names a Persian dialect used in Zoroastrian scriptures, as well as the community itself.

clue.text: Energy shown by pair absorbing new verse

parts.note: go means energy or vigour, as in 'full of go'

indicators.note: absorbing means taking in, so the word for pair holds the next letter

parts.note: a duo is a pair

V is the abbreviation for verse

explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer with no definition and no superfluous letter: Boris Godunov, the Russian tsar, and Mussorgsky's opera about him.
explanation.definitionFit: The theme is the first name Boris, and Boris Godunov ruled Russia as tsar from 1598 to 1605.

clue.text: Men, we hear, supporting US composer getting artificial aid

parts.note: Philip Glass, the American minimalist composer

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by its sound when spoken

parts.note: with its N superfluous the word is me, which is I

explanation.walkthrough: The N of 'Men' is this clue's superfluous letter, leaving me. In a down clue the second piece sits below the first, so it is supporting it.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass eye is an artificial replacement for a lost eye, a prosthesis, though it gives no sight.

clue.text: Children held up, lined among the Spanish as a feature of entry?

parts.note: a brood is a family of young children

indicators.note: among puts the letter inside the Spanish word

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
with its D superfluous the word is line, abbreviated L

explanation.definitionFit: A doorbell is fitted beside a front door so visitors can ring for admission, so it belongs to an entrance.

clue.text: Big cheese possibly seen touring small US state is like a venomous sort?

RI is Rhode Island, the smallest US state

explanation.definitionFit: Viperine means like or relating to vipers, the venomous snakes, so it describes something resembling a poisonous kind.

clue.text: UN study largely wrong about India? Such is barely evident
